title: An Ocean on Mars? Shalbatana Vallis Holds Clues in Its Flood-Carved Depths
summary:
Mars Express, the European Space Agency's veteran orbiter, has turned its high-resolution stereo camera on Shalbatana Vallis — an immense channel that stretches 1,300 kilometers across the Martian equator, roughly the length of Italy. The latest images focus on the valley's northern reaches, revealing a landscape sculpted by ancient cataclysms. Scientists believe that around 3.5 billion years ago, vast reservoirs of groundwater burst onto the surface, unleashing floods that tore through the terrain and carved a channel up to 10 kilometers wide and 500 meters deep.

The valley's floor tells a complex story. A conspicuous blue-black patch is interpreted as volcanic ash, later redistributed by wind. Surrounding the main channel is chaotic terrain — a jumble of broken blocks, ridges, and mounds that formed when subsurface ice melted and the overlying ground collapsed. Similar chaotic landscapes have been observed elsewhere on Mars, including Pyrrhae Regio and Aram Chaos. The region also bears the scars of volcanism: wrinkle ridges hint at ancient lava flows that cooled and crumpled, while isolated mesas are eroded remnants of older highlands.

Perhaps most tantalizing is Shalbatana Vallis's destination. It empties into Chryse Planitia, one of the lowest regions on Mars, where many of the planet's major outflow channels converge. This has led some researchers to propose that Chryse Planitia once contained a large ocean during a warmer, wetter epoch. If true, Shalbatana Vallis was a river-like artery feeding that primordial sea. The new images, combined with topographic data, strengthen the case for a hydrologically active early Mars.

Since arriving in 2003, Mars Express has mapped the planet in unprecedented detail, and its HRSC camera — developed by the German Aerospace Center — continues to deliver. These observations not only illuminate Mars's watery past but also guide future missions searching for signs of ancient life. As scientists parse the valley's layered history, each image brings us closer to answering the big question: was Mars once a living world?
why_it_matters: If Mars once had an ocean, it might have harbored life, and studying its ancient waterways can inform our understanding of climate change and habitability on Earth.

background_read: The European Space Agency (ESA, a collaboration of 22 European nations) launched the Mars Express orbiter in 2003, and it has been mapping the Red Planet ever since. Its HRSC (High Resolution Stereo Camera), built by the German Aerospace Center (DLR, Germany's national space agency), has revealed stunning 3D details of the surface.

Shalbatana Vallis is one of many massive outflow channels that cut across the Martian equator, thought to have formed when underground water reservoirs suddenly burst out around 3.5 billion years ago. Its destination, Chryse Planitia, is a vast lowland basin where several such channels converge.

Some scientists have long hypothesized that this region once held an ocean, making it a prime target in the search for ancient Martian life. Evidence for water on early Mars has accumulated since the 1970s, when Mariner 9 and Viking orbiters first photographed what looked like dried river valleys.

Today, high-resolution instruments like those on Mars Express help researchers piece together the planet's climatic history and evaluate its potential for having hosted living organisms. The images also guide future rovers seeking biosignatures in ancient sediments.

perspectives.description: Evidence for a Martian ocean supports the idea that Mars was once habitable, fueling excitement for upcoming missions like the European ExoMars rover that will drill for organic traces.
The ocean hypothesis is still debated; cratering data and some mineralogy suggest only episodic wet periods, not a stable ocean. A few researchers argue these channels could be volcanic in origin.
Outflow channels and chaotic terrain appear across Mars, indicating that subsurface water and ice played a major role in shaping the planet's surface, regardless of whether a global ocean existed.
High-resolution stereo imaging and future sample return missions could reveal biosignatures preserved in ancient sediments, potentially answering whether life ever existed on Mars.
